issues.issue: The parenthetical list of privileges ends in "etc.", leaving the reach of the general category uncertain, and "properly entitled" is not tied to any stated criterion.
"Encouraging, enticing, influencing or enlisting" — particularly "influencing" — has no boundary, and the prohibition extends to unspecified "other official University documents".

The prohibited behaviours are one-word abstractions — "intimidates", "harasses", "invades personal privacy" — with no definition, so what conduct counts as an invasion of personal privacy or intimidation is genuinely contestable. "Endangers the ... welfare of any other person or oneself on or off campus" has no discernible outer limit.

The closing sentence permits emergency suspension of any student "involved in such an incident" pending investigation, which cannot be squared with Section 22.2's rule that a student's status shall not be altered pending final action except for reasons of imminent danger.
"Comply with instructions of University officials" is unqualified: it names no limit on which officials, which instructions, or whether the instruction must be lawful or reasonable.
"Or other authorized functions" is a catch-all sitting after the enumerated teaching, research, administrative, public service and disciplinary functions, leaving its reach uncertain.
"Causes disruption to or invades another individual's privacy" is undefined, and "misuse" of devices with photographic or messaging capability supplies no standard for what use is permitted.
The final sentence prohibits "issuing any type of threat" — an unbounded phrase dropped into a provision otherwise about fire and safety equipment, so its scope is unclear.

The protected categories listed here differ from the lists in Sections 7.0, 7.1 and 7.3 (e.g. "gender identity and expression" and "veteran status" are stated differently, and only 7.0 adds "any other category protected by law"), leaving the covered classes inconsistent across the instrument.

The definition of hazing — "initiating or disciplining fellow students, often in the nature of forced alcohol consumption, humiliating or painful ordeals" — uses "often" rather than a defining criterion, so the elements of the offence cannot be identified from the text.

"Other articles or substances usable as weapons" is a general catch-all following a specific enumeration of firearms, explosives, knives and fireworks; almost any object is "usable as a weapon", so the ejusdem generis reach of the phrase is genuinely contestable.

As written the first sentence bars bringing "any dog or animal" onto campus "without a leash", while the guide-and-service-animal exception is attached only to the second sentence, so it is unclear whether service animals are exempt from the leash rule.

The sentence is syntactically tangled — "responsibility for the actions, damage, or injuries caused by, or costs incurred for the services related to hosting a guest" — leaving it unclear whether the host is liable for all a guest's acts or only for identified costs.

The provision incorporates by reference an open-ended set of "other official University publications and documents" with only illustrative examples, leaving the body of binding regulation unidentified.

The section is written in hortatory terms — conduct "could be defined as sexual misconduct", students are "encouraged" to communicate — while purporting to state the consent standard, so whether it creates an operative rule and what that rule is are both open.

The closing sentence allows emergency suspension of any student merely "accused of sexual misconduct" pending investigation, which conflicts with Section 22.2's requirement that status not be altered pending final action absent imminent danger.

"Sexual misconduct" is defined only circularly and permissively (contact without explicit consent "may be considered" misconduct), and "explicit consent", "physically or mentally incapacitated" and the presumption raised by mere "evidence of ingestion" each admit of more than one reasonable reading.
The requirement of "explicit consent" cannot be squared with Section 3.3, which provides that consent "may be communicated verbally or through actions".
"Taking advantage of someone's incapacitation or intoxication" is undefined, and it treats mere intoxication as sufficient without saying what taking advantage means.

This provision makes sexual activity with a merely intoxicated person misconduct, while Section 3.1 provides that only a person "physically or mentally incapacitated" is incapable of consent — the two set different thresholds.

"Advantage gained by the accuser's mental or physical incapacity or impairment of which the accused was aware or should have been aware" imports an undefined constructive-knowledge standard, and "impairment" is nowhere bounded.
Permitting consent to be communicated "through actions" conflicts with Section 3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" that is "clearly communicated".

The flat statement that the accuser "will be informed of the outcome" sits against Section 23.O.2, under which final sanction determinations are communicated to the accuser only "in some cases", and against the confidentiality of hearing records in Section 19.14.
"The highest standards of academic integrity" and "or other sanctions" set no ascertainable standard or limit on penalty.

The exception is mis-drafted: work must be "produced without the assistance of others, except for quotation marks, references, and footnotes", which are not forms of assistance, so what collaboration or source use is actually permitted is unclear.

Providing one's own work "through negligence" to assist another student is an offence with no stated standard of care, and the section both authorises joint work and forbids collaboration without explicit permission.
"In identical or similar form" gives no measure of how much similarity converts permissible reuse into an infraction.

The section promises "the policies outlined below" and "guidelines for event sponsorship", but the instrument as reproduced contains no such policies between 5.0 and 5.5, so the obligation it imposes has no referent.
"Abuse of legally-obtained drugs or substances" and "misuse of prescription drugs" are not defined, and "other drug paraphernalia" is a catch-all after "bongs, pipes".
"Spaces designated for that purpose" and "appropriate posting materials" are undefined, and the prohibited-location list ends with "etc."
"Inappropriate use of property" sits as an open-ended term at the end of a list of specific wrongs (vandalism, theft, destruction, damage), leaving its reach uncertain.
"Mistreatment of animals, trees, or plantings" and the duty to "respect and preserve" plant life supply no ascertainable standard of conduct.

"Qualified special, disabled veteran or other eligible veteran status" is garbled, and the list closes with "any other category protected by law", so the protected classes are both mis-stated and open-ended.
The protected-class list here differs from those in Sections 2.7, 7.1 and 7.3, which omit or add categories, so the instrument does not define its protected classes consistently.

Harassment is defined by "the purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering" with education or work by creating an "intimidating, hostile or offensive environment", a standard that turns entirely on undefined and subjective terms.

The protected-class list in this section omits "gender identity and expression", which Sections 2.7 and 7.0 include, leaving the classes covered by the harassment prohibition inconsistent with the non-discrimination policy.
The examples are prefaced by "depending on the circumstances" and "includes, but is not limited to", so the enumerated specifics neither define nor limit what constitutes sexual harassment.

The list ends with the catch-all "other verbal or physical conduct that denigrates or shows hostility or aversion", is expressly "not an exhaustive list", and the closing sentence reserves power to act on whatever the University "deems to be inappropriate" — so the prohibition has no fixed boundary.
"Falsified a claim" is undefined and does not distinguish a knowingly false complaint from one that is simply unsubstantiated, a distinction with real consequences given the sanction of dismissal.
"Other non-University related purposes" is a general catch-all appended to the specific "commercial, political", leaving unclear what other purposes are caught.

The historical recital about the 1947 name change is followed by an operative permission limited to recognised student organisations, and the two do not obviously connect; the heading also promises guidelines on "University Facilities" that the paragraph does not supply.

"Malicious or unauthorized entry" into "personal files, electronic files ... drawers, or locked spaces, such as lockers, etc." ends in an open "etc." and gives no standard for what authorisation means.

The absolute statement that the privacy of every individual's room "must be respected" sits against Section 17.3, which permits periodic staff inspections of residence hall rooms without the occupant present.

The exception is defined by reference to "circumstances as outlined in Section 10.5", a section not contained in this instrument, so the scope of the permission requirement cannot be determined from the document.

Routine inspections "to check for illegal possession of University-owned property" look functionally like searches, yet Section 17.2 requires advance written permission specifying purpose and location for any entry to search a student's room.
"In a timely manner" and "not reported in a timely fashion" set a limitation on complaints with no period attached, so whether a report is time-barred is entirely open.

The statement that discipline "may be implemented only though referral" to DSRCS conflicts with Sections 22.3 and 22.4, under which the Dean may indefinitely suspend or dismiss a student without any DSRCS referral and expressly outside Section 19.

The mediated outcome is described as "final, and binding", yet Section 18.2 provides that failure to adhere to it may lead to further mediation or referral to the conduct process, so the finality of the resolution is not consistent across the two paragraphs.

Outcomes must respect the "parameters found in Section 21", but Section 21 governs sanctions imposed after a responsibility finding, not negotiated restitution, so which parameters bind a mediated outcome is unclear.

The 48-hour clock runs from "delivery" to any of four channels including a campus mailbox and home address, without saying when delivery is deemed effective, and "extenuating circumstances" is undefined.

Deeming a student's silence for 48 hours an "acceptance of responsibility for the violation" cannot easily be reconciled with Section 19.12, which places the burden of proof on the accuser, or with 19.13's requirement that findings rest on evidence.

This provision defines "class days" to include final exams and Senior Week and to exclude summer instruction, while Section 19.6 gives a different definition of the excluded summer period and adds study abroad, so the same term is measured two ways in adjacent sections.

The paragraph both authorises the administrator to decide in the student's absence and guarantees "the right to one rescheduled meeting" for a non-fault absence, without saying which applies first, and the fault determination is left to the same administrator.

"Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter dependent upon the conduct of the accused student" states no criterion or decision-maker, and "if agreed upon by consent of the accuser, and/or the DSRCS administrator, and the accused" leaves whose consent is needed genuinely unclear.

Two retention periods are stated — five years from the case outcome and, "in all cases", five years from the last conduct action — and the "extraordinary cases as defined by the Dean" exception is undefined.

"Within 30 class days, or as soon as practicable" makes the deadline unenforceable on its face, and the prohibition on the parties "confronting or questioning the witnesses and accusers ... prior to the hearing" is broad enough to bar ordinary pre-hearing preparation.

This section lets "the accused and accuser" agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition, while Section 20.2 requires that any waiver of the voting requirements be by mutual consent of the SCB as well as the accuser and accused.

"Passive assistance", "exceptional circumstances" permitting "active participation", and "coexisting criminal charges ... pending resulting from the same incident" are all undefined, so the permitted role of an adviser or of counsel is genuinely contestable.

The Section 3 services text states that this section "permits the passive assistance of legal counsel by either party but only if coexisting criminal charges are pending", whereas 19.8 says such assistance "may be allowed" — a right in one place, a discretion in the other.

The mandatory "must be present at the hearing" is hard to reconcile with Section 19.15, which contemplates non-attendance and treats it as acceptance of responsibility, and with 19.11's allowance of written testimony from absentee witnesses.

"Proof of authorship but not content of such testimony must be made by certification of a notary public" is garbled, and "the right to question all witnesses appearing before the Board and only at the hearing" is ambiguous as to whether "only at the hearing" limits the right or the occasion.
The guarantee of a right to question "all witnesses" cannot be squared with the same paragraph's and Section 19.9's acceptance of written testimony from absentee witnesses who never appear.

Placing the burden of proof on "the accuser" is difficult to reconcile with Sections 19.1 and 19.15, which deem responsibility accepted when the accused misses a deadline or a hearing, and with 19.13, which requires findings to rest on evidence introduced at the hearing.

The provision fixes two different standards of proof in the same paragraph — "clear and convincing evidence" generally and preponderance for Section 3 or 7 allegations — without saying which governs a case charging both kinds of violation.

The footnote to Section 23 says hearing procedures "may differ" in sexual misconduct cases in accordance with Title IX, leaving it uncertain whether 19.13's standards and voting rules survive in exactly those cases the note singles out.

"Through no fault of his/her own as determined by the DSRCS hearing administrator" makes the same officer the sole judge of fault, with no stated criteria, and the consequence is automatic acceptance of responsibility.

Deeming an absent student to have accepted responsibility and referring the case "for administrative action (see Section 19.3)" conflicts both with 19.12's placement of the burden on the accuser and with 19.3, which by its terms applies only to students who chose administrative action.

The four enumerated appeal grounds are exclusive ("based only on") and appeals may not rest on "dissatisfaction with an imposed sanction", yet a successful appeal produces a wholly new hearing at which the Board may increase or decrease the sanction — the reach of the grounds against that de novo remedy is genuinely contestable.

This section makes sanctions effective on approval by "the Dean of Student Life ... or the Director", while Section 21.1 provides that sanctions take effect on approval by the Director or the Associate Dean and that only suspensions and dismissals require the Dean.

The two-class-day window here is far shorter than the seven days allowed for board appeals in Section 19.16, and it is unclear how the Dean's review interacts with the Section 19.16 appeal route for cases referred to administrative action under 19.15.

Requiring a student to seek a continuance rather than raise new evidence later reads as a waiver, which is hard to square with Section 19.16.d's express appeal ground of "new evidence not previously available".

Waiver of the voting composition requires "mutual consent of the SCB, the accuser, and the accused", whereas Section 19.7 permits the accused and accuser alone to agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum composition.

This section states that "An Associate Dean of Student Life will serve as chairperson of the University Appeals Board", while Section 20.8 provides for "one faculty chairperson" who must be a full-time tenured faculty member appointed by the Dean of Student Life.
The requirement of a full-time tenured faculty chairperson directly contradicts Section 20.7, which provides that an Associate Dean of Student Life will chair the University Appeals Board.

Requiring the Hearing Administrator to serve "in all stages ... including hearings and deliberations" and to advise the Board sits uneasily with Section 19.6, which says the administrator is non-voting and "will not act in any way to influence the outcome of a case".

The sanctioning factors and the "learning components" are both introduced by "including but not limited to", so the enumerated items neither confine the discretion nor identify what else may be imposed; "failure in a course" is listed as a learning component.

The approval chain here (Director or Associate Dean, with the Dean for suspensions and dismissals) does not match Section 19.16, which conditions effectiveness of any sanction on approval or modification by the Dean of Student Life or the Director.
The privileges that may be withdrawn are "including, but not limited to" a list of specific ones, so the sanction has no defined outer boundary.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certificates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is plainly corrupt — words have dropped out — so the duration and effect of a suspension cannot be read off the text.

"May take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable", closing with "other action deemed necessary", is a wholly open-ended grant of power triggered by an undefined "significant threat" to "emotional ... well-being".

The unlimited power to act on a perceived threat cannot be reconciled with Section 22.2, which provides that pending final action a student's status "shall not be altered" except for reasons of imminent danger.

Making the Dean "the only authorized grantor of permission" to return is in tension with Section 22.5, which conditions resumption of campus functions on the Dean "or designee", and with 21.1's allocation of sanction approval to the Director and Associate Dean.
"Imminent danger to their physical or emotional safety or well-being" is an undefined and highly elastic trigger for removing a student from campus.

The rule that status shall not be altered pending final action except for imminent danger conflicts with Sections 3.0 and 2.1.f, which permit emergency suspension of any student merely accused of misconduct, and with 22.3, which permits indefinite suspension on a criminal charge without any imminent-danger finding.

"Charged with or convicted of a crime" is not limited by seriousness or jurisdiction, and the provision gives no standard for how the Dean is to weigh "the nature of the crime" against the risk to the community.

The statement that "the procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply" removes the entire conduct process, contradicting Section 18.0's rule that discipline may be implemented only through DSRCS referral and Section 22.2's imminent-danger precondition for separating a student.

"Behavior that is inconsistent with this expectation and adversely affects the University community", judged solely "in the judgment of the Dean", sets no ascertainable standard for conduct that can lead to dismissal.

Excluding Section 19 from all off-campus conduct cannot be reconciled with Section 18.0, which permits discipline only through referral to DSRCS, or with 2.1.f, which expressly brings off-campus endangerment within the ordinary conduct process.

The absolute exclusion from campus with "no exception for examinations" is difficult to square with the preceding paragraph of 22.5, which gives the student three class days to contest the protocol and the Dean discretion to restore privileges.

The enumerated "rights to fairness" are stated in bare terms — "to question witnesses appearing against them", "to submit verbal arguments" — without saying whether they are enforceable entitlements or merely a script the chairperson reads.

These stated rights are undercut by the footnote to Section 23, which provides that hearing procedures "may differ" in sexual misconduct cases, and by Section 19.6's bar on questioning witnesses before the hearing.

"In alphabetical order" does not say alphabetical by what, and "this system shall prevail throughout the remainder of the hearing procedures" leaves unclear which of the two options (individually or as a group) is fixed for the rest of the hearing.

"Hearing procedures may differ ... in accordance with Title IX" identifies no procedure that may change, no decision-maker, and no limit, so it is impossible to tell from the text what process applies in a sexual misconduct case.

This footnote licenses departure from the detailed hearing steps of Section 23 and, on its face, from the procedural guarantees of Sections 19.6 to 19.13 and the statement of rights in 23.C, in precisely the class of cases those provisions expressly address.

Communicating the outcome to the accuser only "in some cases" conflicts with the Section 3 services provision, which states flatly that "the accuser will be informed of the outcome of disciplinary proceedings in which sexual assault is alleged".
